title: How we speak: the Craveiral voice
vimeoName: Belong School · Module 11 · How We Speak

segments.text: This module is about words. It might seem like a strange training topic,
but you'll use words with guests hundreds of times a day, and the words we choose
are as much a part of Craveiral as the pine trees.
A place that talks about the rhythm of the land in the tone of an airport
announcement is a place at war with itself.
So, the Craveiral voice. The principle first: our voice
is calm, warm, concrete, and unhurried, like the place.
We don't gush, we don't perform enthusiasm, we don't sound like a script.
We sound like a person from this land who is glad you came and knows things worth
knowing. That's it. If you're ever unsure how to say something, say it the way
you'd say it to a friend's parents visiting your home. Respectful, warm, real.
Now, some vocabulary, because small word choices carry the whole philosophy.
We say houses, not units or rooms.
Guests sleep in a house with a kitchen and a terrace. The word should honor that.
We say guests, never clients or customers. We covered why.
We say the farm because it is one. A real working farm, not grounds or
landscaping. We say the farm table, and we talk about dishes by where they came
from, not just what they are. And notice the words the brand lives by.
Belong, stay, the rhythm of the land, root to table, the chain.
Use them naturally when they're true, never as decoration.
The same care applies in reverse. Words we avoid: anything that makes us
sound like a resort chain. Amenity, property features, valued guest.
Corporate language is a wall between two people.
Our whole project is taking walls down. And avoid over-promising words.
Perfect, guaranteed, always. The Alentejo has weather. Farms have seasons.
Kitchens have nights. Promise what we control: care, honesty, effort.
Those we can always deliver. Speaking with international guests, and most of our
guests are international. German, Dutch, French, British, American.
Three notes. First, keep English simple and warm.
You don't need perfect grammar, you need clear goodwill.
A genuine, let me find out for you, beats fluent evasion in any language.
Second, teach a little Portuguese when the moment invites it.
Guests love leaving with obrigado, bom dia, the story of the word Craveiral itself.
A field of carnations. It's a gift that costs nothing.
Third, cultures differ in what warmth looks like.
Some guests want conversation. Others want efficiency and privacy.
Both deserve the same care, calibrated. Reading that difference is a skill.
Watch your most experienced colleagues do it. Writing.
Some of you write to guests, emails, messages, responses to questions.
Same voice on paper. Short sentences.
Warm but never syrupy, always concrete.
Not, we look forward to welcoming you soon, as an empty formula, but,
"The pool is heated in October and the trails are at their best.
You're coming at a lovely time." One true, specific sentence outperforms three
ornamental ones, every time. And how we speak to each other.
Because the internal voice becomes the external one, always.
Teams that speak to each other with respect serve guests with grace.
Teams that bark at each other backstage leak that tension into the dining room
within a week. Guests feel it before they can name it.
So, no shouting culture, not even in the kitchen at full throttle. Direct is good.
Sharp is fine under pressure. Disrespectful is never fine.
Disagree openly, decide, move. I'd rather hear an honest, this
isn't working, in a team meeting than a polite silence that costs us a season.
One more thing. How we talk about Craveiral when we're not at Craveiral.
Each of you is the brand at a dinner table, on your own social media, in the
village café. I'm not going to police that. I wouldn't want to.
I'll only say, the stories you tell about this place are the most credible
marketing we will ever have. Infinitely more than anything we buy.
Tell the true ones, including the funny ones, especially the funny ones.
Words, in the end, are hospitality's smallest unit. A stay is thousands of them.
Choose them the way the kitchen chooses tomatoes.
In season, close to home, and real.
Last module coming up,
and it's the one I care most about getting right.
How we lead, how we work together, and what I expect from you.
And you should expect from me.
